COMPTROLLER’S DECISION

This decision is considered final on February 5, 2024, unless a motion for rehearing is timely filed; this date of finality is calculated based on the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).[1] The failure to timely file a motion for rehearing may result in adverse legal consequences.

Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Kathy Pickup of the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) issued a Proposal for Decision (PFD) that includes Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law. SOAH served the PFD on each party and each party was given an opportunity to file exceptions and replies with SOAH in accordance with SOAH’s rules of procedure. The ALJ recommended that the Comptroller adopt the PFD as written.

After review and consideration, IT IS ORDERED that the PFD is adopted as changed.[2]

The result from this Decision is Attachment A. The ALJ’s recommendation letter is Attachment B. The PFD as changed is Attachment C. Attachments A, B, and C are incorporated by reference.

Attachment A reflects a liability.[3]

The total sum of the tax, penalty, and interest is due and payable 20 days after a comptroller’s decision becomes final.[4] If such sum is not timely paid, an additional penalty of 10 percent of the taxes due will accrue.

TAXPAYER NO: ***************

v.

TEXAS COMPTROLLER OF PUBLIC ACCOUNTS

BEFORE THE STATE OFFICE OF ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS

Proposal for Decision

The Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) audited *************** (Petitioner) for compliance with sales and use tax laws and made an assessment that included tax, 10% late penalty, and accrued interest. Petitioner asked for redetermination contending it performed its own analysis with additional documentation and its results differ from the auditor’s results and that deposits of personal funds were recorded as sales. Additionally, Petitioner contends its delivery service collected tax, but it did not report these sales as taxable sales. Petitioner believes it is owed money from the State. In this Proposal for Decision, the Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) finds that the audit assessment should be upheld, except as agreed by Staff.

I. NOTICE, JURISDICTION, AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY

Staff referred the contested case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH) and, on September 21, 2023, issued a Notice of Hearing by Written Submission to Petitioner. On September 25, 2023, ALJ Kathy Pickup issued Order Setting Written Submission Requirements which set the written submission hearing. Petitioner was represented by ***************. James Sutton represented Staff. The contested case record closed on December 4, 2023.

There are no issues of notice or jurisdiction; therefore, those matters are set out in the Findings of Fact and Conclusions of Law without further discussion.

II. REASONS FOR DECISION

A. Evidence Presented

Petitioner provided a Sales Tax Report for the period March 1, 2015, to September 30, 2018. Staff provided the pleadings the parties exchanged prior to referring the matter to SOAH and submitted the following exhibits:

1. Hearing Request Receipt;

2. Texas Notification of Audit Results;

3. Penalty & Interest Waiver Worksheet;

4. Audit Report;

5. Audit Plan;

6. Petitioner Letter Dated March 9, 2020; and

7. Petitioner Documents Dated September 10, 2020.

The Parties’ exhibits were admitted into the record without objection.

B. Agreed Adjustments

Staff agreed to waive interest from January 1, 2021, to August 31, 2023.

C. Facts Established and Issues Presented

During the period at issue, Petitioner operated a pizza restaurant in CITY, Texas. Petitioner’s tax permit was inactive as of October 31, 2019. In November 2018, Staff initiated a sales and use tax compliance audit of Petitioner for the period March 1, 2015, through September 30, 2018. Petitioner provided financial statements, tax workpapers, sales journals, federal income tax returns, sales invoices, bank statements, general ledgers, depreciation schedules, voucher register/journal, and purchase invoices.

On May 17, 2019, Staff issued Petitioner a Notification of Audit Results assessing tax, 10% late penalty, and interest accrued to the account. Petitioner requested redetermination, contending it performed its own analysis using additional documentation with its results differing from the auditor’s results and that deposits of personal funds were recorded as sales. Additionally, Petitioner learned that its delivery service collected tax, but Petitioner did not report the sales as taxable sales. Petitioner believes the state owes it $930.89.

Petitioner represented to the auditor that its point-of-sale system allowed a report to be run for only the prior month. The available information did not detail or identify the amounts Petitioner collected as tax. The auditor therefore deemed much of Petitioner’s documentation unreliable and incomplete due to missing source documents, such as daily invoices and receipts. Due to the incomplete records, the auditor estimated additional taxable sales.

The auditor performed the estimation using the reported gross sales from Petitioner’s 2016 and 2017 federal income tax returns. The auditor divided the reported sales by 24 to estimate monthly sales, and then multiplied the monthly sales by 43, the number of months in the audit period, to determine the total taxable sales. Petitioner’s total reported sales were subtracted from the total taxable sales to determine the additional taxable sales, which were divided by the 43 months in the audit to estimate the additional monthly taxable sales. The auditor multiplied additional taxable sales by the tax rate to estimate the additional tax due. Staff did not agree to adjust the audit and referred the matter to SOAH.

D. ALJ ANALYSIS AND RECOMMENDATION

Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Id. § 151.010. All sellers and all other persons storing, using, or consuming in this state a taxable item purchased from a retailer shall keep records in the form the Comptroller requires. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(a)(1). For example, a seller must keep records of all gross receipts, including documentation in the form of receipts from each sale occurring during each reporting period. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(1). In addition, a seller’s records must substantiate any claimed deductions or exclusions authorized by law. Id. § 151.025(a)(3); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b). If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on the best information available. Tex. Tax Code §§ 111.0042(d), .008(a).

Petitioner disagrees with the audit results and contends that an analysis of its records shows it overpaid tax, personal deposits were treated as transactions, and a delivery service collected tax on sales that were not reported. Petitioner provided a spreadsheet summarizing its documentation but did not provide any source records to support its contentions. A taxpayer cannot defeat an assessment based on the burden of proof by withholding or failing to provide documentation. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 102,386 (2014), 105,892 (2012). Treating transactions that lack documentation as taxable is supported by statute. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 103,035 (2014), 39,765 (2003). Additionally, the Comptroller has routinely held that summary documents that are created by the taxpayer and submitted without underlying support are tantamount to bare assertions, i.e., they are not considered evidence. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 117,167-117,174, 117,168 and 117,169 (2023). Petitioner’s spreadsheet is not supported by any documentation or source records. Petitioner has also not provided documentation to support its contention that the state owes it $930.89.

The audit consisted of one exam, Exam 200, where adjustments were made for additional taxable sales, and which was estimated due to lack of records. Although Petitioner contends that the owner’s bank transfers to the business account were treated as taxable sales, the auditor calculated the assessment using Petitioner’s federal income tax returns and reported taxable sales and did not consider Petitioner’s bank transfers for purposes of calculating the estimated tax due. Petitioner has not demonstrated that its federal reporting was based on, and reconciled with, bank deposits for the period at issue. Staff contends Petitioner’s records were unreliable and incomplete and that, in the absence of reliable records, Petitioner’s federal income tax returns were the best information available. The ALJ agrees. Additionally, Petitioner did not establish that the auditor made assessments for nontaxable revenue, and it failed to produce any additional records to substantiate its contentions or show error in the audit. Staff’s prima facie case to show the transactions were taxable is met.

Petitioner’s evidence is insufficient to demonstrate, by a preponderance of evidence, that any items in dispute were scheduled erroneously. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e). Petitioner’s contentions should be denied, and the audit assessment should be upheld, except as agreed by Staff.

III. FINDINGS OF FACT

1. During the period at issue, *************** (Petitioner) operated a pizza restaurant in CITY, Texas.

2. Petitioner’s tax permit was inactive as of October 31, 2019.

3. In November 2018, the Tax Division (Staff) of the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (Comptroller) initiated a sales tax compliance audit of Petitioner for the period March 1, 2015, through September 30, 2018.

4. Petitioner provided financial statements, tax workpapers, sales journals, federal income tax returns, sales invoices, bank statements, general ledgers, depreciation schedules, voucher register/journal, and purchase invoices.

5. On May 17, 2019, Staff issued Petitioner a Notification of Audit Results assessing tax, 10% late penalty, and interest accrued to the account.

6. Petitioner timely requested redetermination.

7. Petitioner represented to the auditor that its point-of-sale system allowed a report to be run for only the prior month. The available information did not detail or identify the amounts Petitioner collected as tax.

8. The auditor deemed much of Petitioner’s documentation unreliable and incomplete due to missing source documents, such as daily invoices and receipts.

9. Due to the incomplete records, the auditor estimated additional taxable sales.

10. The auditor performed the estimation using the reported gross sales from Petitioner’s 2016 and 2017 federal income tax returns.

11. The auditor divided the reported sales by 24 to estimate monthly sales, and then multiplied the monthly sales by 43, the number of months in the audit period, to determine the total taxable sales.

12. Petitioner’s total reported sales were subtracted from the total taxable sales to determine the additional taxable sales, which were divided by the 43 months in the audit to estimate the additional monthly taxable sales.

13. The auditor multiplied additional taxable sales by the tax rate to estimate the additional tax due. Staff referred the contested case to the State Office of Administrative Hearings (SOAH).

14. The contested case record closed on December 4, 2023.

15. Staff agreed to waive interest from January 1, 2021, to August 31, 2023.

IV. CONCLUSIONS OF LAW

1. The Comptroller has jurisdiction over this matter pursuant to Texas Tax Code ch. 111.

2. SOAH has jurisdiction over matters related to this hearing, including the authority to issue a proposal for decision with findings of fact and conclusions of law. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2003.

3. Staff provided proper and timely notice of the hearing. Tex. Gov’t Code ch. 2001; Tex. Tax Code § 111.009.

4. Texas imposes a tax on each sale of a taxable item in this state. Tex. Tax Code § 151.051.

5. The term “taxable item” includes tangible personal property and taxable services. Tex. Tax Code § 151.010.

6. All sellers and all other persons storing, using, or consuming in this state a taxable item purchased from a retailer shall keep records in the form the Comptroller requires. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(a)(1).

7. For example, a seller must keep records of all gross receipts, including documentation in the form of receipts from each sale occurring during each reporting period. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(1).

8. A seller’s records must substantiate any claimed deductions or exclusions authorized by law. Tex. Tax Code § 151.025(a)(3); 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 3.281(b).

9. If a taxpayer fails to keep accurate records of gross receipts, gross purchases, deductions, and exclusions, the Comptroller may take actions that include estimating the person’s tax liability based on the best information available. Tex. Tax Code §§ 111.0042(d), .008(a).

10. A taxpayer cannot defeat an assessment based on the burden of proof by withholding or failing to provide documentation. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 102,386 (2014), 105,892 (2012).

11. Treating transactions that lack documentation as taxable is supported by statute. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 103,035 (2014), 39,765 (2003).

12. The Comptroller has routinely held that summary documents that are created by the taxpayer and submitted without underlying support are tantamount to bare assertions, i.e., they are not considered evidence. See, e.g., Comptroller’s Decision Nos. 117,167-117,174 117,168, and 117,169(2023).

13. Petitioner’s records were unreliable and incomplete and, in the absence of reliable records, Petitioner’s federal income tax returns were the best information available.

14. Staff’s prima facie case to show the transactions were taxable is met.

15. Petitioner’s evidence is insufficient to demonstrate, by a preponderance of evidence, that any remaining items in dispute were scheduled erroneously. 34 Tex. Admin. Code § 1.26(e).

16. Petitioner’s contentions should be denied.

17. The audit assessment should be upheld, except as agreed by Staff.

SIGNED December 5, 2023.

KATHY PICKUP

PRESIDING ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE

ENDNOTES:

[1] The date calculated is 25 days after this decision is signed. See APA, Tex. Gov’t Code § 2001.146(a); S.B. 1095, Acts 2017, 85th Leg. For additional guidance, refer to the Frequently Asked Questions Related to Motions for Rehearing, found here: http://comptroller.texas.gov/taxes/publications/96-1789.pdf

[2] See Tex. Gov’t Code § 2003.101(e) and (f).

[3] At present, insufficient information is available to determine which items and amounts are disputed or undisputed for purposes of Tex. Tax Code, Ch. 112. In the absence of this information, the Comptroller will assume the entire amount of the assessment, as it appears in Comptroller’s Decision Attachment A, the Notification of Hearing Results, remains in dispute. If Petitioner intends to sue the comptroller to dispute an amount of tax, penalty, or interest assessed in a deficiency redetermination or jeopardy determination under Tex. Tax Code, Ch. 111, Petitioner is required to file a motion for rehearing that “states the specific grounds of error and the disputed amounts associated with the grounds of error.” Tex. Tax Code § 112.201(a)(3). Petitioner should refer to Tex. Tax Code, Ch. 112, for further guidance regarding a suit after redetermination.

[4] See Tex. Tax Code § 111.0081(c).
